The 'informal economy paradox' highlights that in many developing countries informal workers are not primarily the marginalized poor: micro-surveys in Peru and Mexico found that many informal workers earn more than formal sector workers after accounting for taxes, social contributions, and regulations; informality can be rational exit from burdensome formality.

The 'climate Minsky moment' — a sudden repricing of carbon-intensive assets when climate policy tightens or physical risks materialize — is identified by central banks as a systemic financial stability risk; fossil fuel company equity could lose 40–80% of its value if a Paris-consistent carbon price were implemented suddenly.

The 'rentier capitalism' thesis, advanced by Colin Crouch and others, describes how major corporations in digital platforms, finance, and pharmaceuticals extract economic rents from intellectual property and network monopolies rather than competing through innovation; it is proposed as a structural explanation for the simultaneous rise in corporate profitability and decline in productive investment.

The 'economic geography of health' shows massive within-country disparities: in the U.S., life expectancy varies by over 20 years between the most and least affluent counties; in the UK, men in Blackpool live 10 fewer years than men in Kensington; these geographic health inequalities largely reflect underlying economic inequality and labor market conditions.

The 'Prebisch-Keynes' international monetary reform proposals at Bretton Woods differed dramatically: Keynes wanted a global clearing union with an 'bancor' reserve currency and penalties on surplus nations; the U.S. (White Plan) prevailed, creating dollar dominance; Keynes's balanced adjustment mechanism might have prevented the persistent global imbalances that followed.

The 'price of inequality' thesis (Stiglitz, 2012) argues that rising inequality in the U.S. slows economic growth by reducing consumer demand, distorting political priorities toward the interests of the wealthy, and misallocating talent away from productive work toward rent extraction; it challenges the view that inequality is an acceptable price for dynamism.

The 'global care chains' phenomenon describes how wealthy families in rich countries pay immigrant women to care for their children and elderly parents, while those immigrant women leave their own children in the care of other, cheaper labor in origin countries — creating transnational chains of care commodification that expose the limits of care markets.

The 'Prebisch-Fajnzylber' analysis of Latin American innovation found that the region suffered a 'technological deficit' — high dependency on imported technology and low domestic R&D spending — which perpetuated underdevelopment; Fajnzylber's prescription of 'genuine competitiveness' based on productivity rather than wage suppression influenced Chile's and Brazil's industrial policies.

The 'cost of business cycles' — the welfare loss from economic fluctuations — was estimated by Robert Lucas at only 0.05% of consumption (trivially small), suggesting that stabilization policy is less important than growth policy; this controversial finding has been challenged by research showing that recessions have permanent 'hysteresis' effects on long-run growth.

The 'Prebisch-Thirlwall' balance-of-payments constrained growth model argues that a country's long-run growth rate is constrained by the need to keep imports in line with export growth; this 'Thirlwall's Law' predicts that countries with high income elasticity of import demand and low income elasticity of export demand will grow more slowly — consistent with observations on Latin America.

The 'degrowth vs. green growth debate' is one of the sharpest in environmental economics: mainstream economists (IPCC, IEA) argue technological progress can decouple GDP growth from carbon emissions, while ecological economists argue absolute decoupling at the required scale is empirically unobserved and politically unlikely — making degrowth in rich nations necessary.

The 'Prebisch-North-Thomas' institutional efficiency theory argued that feudal institutions — protecting lords' rather than peasants' property rights — were economically efficient for elites in low-population, land-abundant medieval Europe; only when the Black Death shifted bargaining power toward laborers did institutional change occur, illustrating how institutions change through shifts in relative bargaining power.

The 'South-South trade' — commerce between developing countries — grew from 8% of world trade in 1990 to over 25% by 2020, driven by China's rise as an industrial exporter and importer of primary commodities; this reconfiguration of global trade flows has reduced developing countries' dependence on OECD markets but created new dependency relationships with China.

Automation of white-collar work — using AI to replace lawyers, accountants, medical diagnosticians, and financial analysts — represents the 'second wave' of labor displacement; Goldman Sachs (2023) estimated AI could automate 25–50% of tasks in most professional occupations, potentially displacing 300 million full-time equivalent jobs globally.

The 'wealth tax debate' intensified after Piketty's work; proposals range from Elizabeth Warren's 2% annual tax on wealth above $50 million to a 1% global wealth tax endorsed by EU leaders in 2024; economists Saez and Zucman estimated a 2% wealth tax on U.S. billionaires could raise $3 trillion over 10 years.

source.name: Gabriel Zucman, University of California Berkeley

text: The 'Prebisch-Aghion' Schumpeterian growth theory reconciles creative destruction with long-run growth: incumbent firms invest in innovation to escape competition from entrants, creating a 'step-by-step' innovation ladder where leapfrogging by far-behind firms is limited; policy implication is that competition policy and patent protection must be carefully balanced.

The 'social infrastructure thesis' of Hall and Jones (1999) found that 'social infrastructure' — institutions and government policies that prevent diversion of resources into unproductive activity — is the primary determinant of cross-country productivity differences, explaining why Western Europe is 4–10 times more productive per worker than Sub-Saharan Africa.

The 'race to the bottom in labor standards' describes competitive pressure on developing countries to maintain low wages and weak environmental standards to attract FDI; the ILO's 'decent work agenda' and the EU's supply chain due diligence directive attempt to establish international floor standards that reduce this race.

The 'crypto-Keynesianism' of COVID-19 fiscal stimulus — direct payments to households via digital transfers — was unprecedented in its speed and scale; the U.S. sent $814 billion in three rounds of 'stimulus checks' to over 160 million Americans; research found these payments reduced poverty by 45% temporarily and created measurable consumption multipliers.

The 'medical bankruptcy' problem — unique to the U.S. among wealthy nations — illustrates market failures in healthcare: approximately 530,000 families file for bankruptcy annually citing medical bills; a single serious illness can cost $500,000+; without universal coverage, medical debt is the leading cause of personal bankruptcy and a major driver of wealth inequality.

The 'economic basis of imperialism' was analyzed by J.A. Hobson (1902) and Lenin (1917) who argued that capitalism's chronic under-consumption forces capital to seek profitable investment abroad, requiring territorial and political control over markets and raw materials; while this thesis has limitations, it influenced 20th century anti-colonial movements.

The 'Prebisch-Reinert' development theory emphasizes that manufacturing activities have higher potential for learning, economies of scale, and technical progress ('Schumpeterian' activities) compared to agriculture or services — explaining why industrializing countries grow faster and why deindustrialization in advanced countries is economically costly.

The 'financial globalization backlash' — capital flow management re-legitimized after 2010 — marked a sea change in IMF orthodoxy; from the 1990s when capital account liberalization was almost universally promoted, the IMF's 2011 'institutional view on capital flows' acknowledged that capital controls can be appropriate policy tools in specific circumstances.

The 'global supply chain revolution' (1990–2020) reduced global manufacturing trade costs by 70% through containerization, ICT coordination, and trade liberalization; it integrated 500 million workers in developing countries into global production networks but also created unprecedented economic interdependence and supply chain fragility.

The 'Prebisch-Kalecki' post-Keynesian theory of income distribution holds that the wage share of national income depends on the degree of monopoly: as markets become more concentrated and markup power increases, profits displace wages; the rise of superstar firms and declining market competition since the 1980s is consistent with this prediction.

The 'economic freedom paradox of Qatar and UAE' illustrates that extreme economic openness can coexist with denial of basic labor rights: 94% of Qatar's workforce consists of migrant workers denied citizenship, facing kafala sponsorship systems that restrict movement; the 2022 FIFA World Cup brought global attention to economic exploitation despite Qatar's high 'economic freedom' rankings.

The 'Prebisch-Taylor' heterodox macroeconomics emphasized the role of distributive conflict — between workers and capitalists over the wage share — in driving inflation and growth dynamics; this 'structuralist' approach to inflation (contrasting with monetarist and demand-pull theories) influenced stabilization policies in Latin America during the 1980s debt crisis.

The 'environmental justice movement' highlights that pollution and environmental harms are not distributed randomly — low-income communities and communities of color disproportionately bear toxic industrial burdens; U.S. studies find that non-white Americans are 40% more likely to live in areas with the worst air quality, linking environmental and economic inequality.

The 'Prebisch-Rodrik' 'trilemma of the world economy' — that deep economic integration, national sovereignty, and democratic politics cannot all coexist — has been partially tested by the Brexit experience: the UK chose national sovereignty over deep EU integration, and voters chose democratic control over technocratic economic management.

The 'universal basic services' concept — proposed as an alternative to Universal Basic Income — argues that providing guaranteed public services (healthcare, education, housing, transport, internet) is more efficient and equitable than cash transfers, because services have economies of scale and address non-income aspects of poverty.

The 'Prebisch-Veblen' conspicuous consumption critique — that the wealthy consume luxury goods to signal status rather than utility, and the middle class imitate them, creating a 'consumption cascade' — was formalized by Thorstein Veblen in 1899 and is now supported by behavioral economics research on positional goods and 'keeping up with the Joneses.'

The 'Nordic paradox' of low inequality and high entrepreneurship challenges the notion that redistribution stifles innovation: Denmark has among the world's highest taxes and most generous welfare states but also among the highest rates of new business formation; economists attribute this to how a strong safety net reduces the risk of entrepreneurial failure.

The 'Prebisch-Walras' general equilibrium theory describes an economy where all markets clear simultaneously through a system of prices coordinated by the 'auctioneer'; Arrow and Debreu (1954) proved the existence of such an equilibrium, but the conditions required (no externalities, complete markets, perfect information) make it an ideal rather than description of reality.

The 'economics of sports' illustrates monopsony power: sports leagues historically used reserve clauses binding players to teams indefinitely; after Curt Flood's challenge led to free agency in baseball (1976), player salaries rose from roughly $50,000 to over $4 million average by 2020 — demonstrating how monopsony suppresses wages below competitive levels.

The 'moral hazard of bailouts' — banks taking excessive risks knowing governments will rescue them — was addressed by the Dodd-Frank Act's 'orderly liquidation authority' and 'living wills' for systemically important banks; however, critics argue the banking sector remains implicitly too big to fail, preserving moral hazard despite regulatory reform.

The 'developmental state' concept — identified by Chalmers Johnson's study of Japan's MITI ministry (1982) — describes an active state that guides private investment toward strategic industries through indicative planning, subsidized credit, and protected markets; South Korea and Taiwan's industrial policies are its most successful examples, producing world-class industries in semiconductors and electronics.

The 'Prebisch-Banerjee' poverty economics insight that the poor pay more for many goods and services — the 'poverty premium' — is documented across housing (higher per-unit costs for small spaces), credit (payday loan APRs of 400%+), and food (premium in food deserts) — making poverty itself expensive in ways that trap people in low-consumption equilibria.

source.name: MIT Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab

text: The 'degrowth of GDP from sustainability' paradox: activities that improve human welfare (volunteering, unpaid care work, ecosystem restoration) reduce GDP, while activities that harm welfare (environmental remediation after pollution, medical treatment of preventable disease) increase it; economists like Stiglitz propose replacing GDP with a 'dashboard' of welfare measures.

source.name: Commission on the Measurement of Economic Performance and Social Progress

text: The 'intangible economy' — where investment in software, R&D, brand equity, and organizational capital exceeds investment in physical capital — now accounts for over 60% of total investment in advanced economies; intangibles have unusual economic properties (scalability, spillovers, synergies, sunkenness) that are reshaping competition, inequality, and macroeconomic dynamics.

The 'Prebisch-Palma' heterodox analysis of income distribution found a remarkable stability in the middle class's income share (deciles 5–9 always capture roughly 50% of national income) while the top 10% and bottom 40% vary enormously across countries and over time — suggesting that inequality is primarily a conflict between the top 10% and the bottom 40%.

The 'China-Africa economic relationship' has transformed since 2000: China is now Africa's largest trading partner and infrastructure financier; Chinese investment built 10,000 km of railways, 100,000 km of roads, and 1,000 bridges across Africa by 2020 — though concerns about debt sustainability, technology transfer terms, and labor practices have grown.

The 'prisoner's dilemma of climate action' — where each country has an incentive not to decarbonize if others don't, even though all would benefit if all decarbonized — is the fundamental challenge of international climate governance; game-theory solutions include trade-linked carbon border tariffs, technology transfer inducements, and large country leadership as focal points.

The 'great wealth transfer' — the intergenerational transfer of approximately $84 trillion in assets from Baby Boomers to Gen X and Millennials in the U.S. over the next 20 years — will reshape wealth distribution; but because Boomer wealth is itself highly concentrated, the transfer will primarily enrich already-wealthy millennials, potentially worsening within-generation inequality.

The 'economics of attention' recognizes that human attention is the scarce resource in the digital economy; platforms compete for attention, which is monetized through advertising; average Americans now spend 4+ hours per day on smartphones; economists like Eli Noam model this 'attention economy' as a market with its own supply and demand dynamics.

The 'Prebisch-Hirschman' linkages theory argued that industrialization proceeds through backward linkages (demand for inputs) and forward linkages (use of outputs) from 'leading sectors'; Hirschman's 'unbalanced growth' strategy — deliberately choosing projects with strong linkages — contrasted with Nurkse's balanced growth approach and was more practical for resource-constrained governments.

The 'monopsony revolution' in labor economics recognizes widespread employer market power beyond obvious cases like company towns; surveys find most U.S. labor markets have only 3–5 major employers per occupation, and job concentration correlates with lower wages; this suggests labor markets are less competitive than assumed and minimum wages may have smaller employment effects.

The 'Prebisch-Amin' theory of unequal exchange argued that trade between developing and developed countries is systematically unfair because labor in peripheral countries is paid below its productivity while core country labor commands a premium through trade unions and political power; Amin estimated that unequal exchange transferred $22 billion per year from periphery to core in the 1970s.

The 'heterodox economics of money creation' — emphasizing that banks create money ex nihilo when they make loans, rather than intermediating existing deposits — has moved from heterodox to mainstream; the Bank of England's 2014 'Money Creation in the Modern Economy' paper explicitly adopted the endogenous money view, with profound implications for monetary policy design.

The 'inclusive capitalism' concept — promoted by the IMF, the World Economic Forum, and investors like Larry Fink — argues that capitalism must become more equitable to remain politically sustainable; ESG investing, stakeholder capitalism, and profit-sharing proposals are practical expressions of this broad sentiment, though economists debate their substantive impact.

The 'Prebisch-Crotty' financial fragility model updates Minsky with the insight that financial innovations — securitization, derivatives, off-balance-sheet vehicles — allow banks to evade capital requirements and take on hidden leverage; this 'endogenous fragility' means that prudential regulation is always running behind financial innovation.

The 'economic populism cycle' — where populist governments (Chávez, Perón, Morales) win elections by promising redistribution and consumption booms, generate short-term growth, but ultimately collapse into hyperinflation and fiscal crisis — was documented by Dornbusch and Edwards (1991) as a recurring Latin American pattern.

The 'Prebisch-Minsky' financial instability in developing countries takes the form of capital flow cycles: boom periods of capital inflow, currency appreciation, credit expansion, and optimism are followed by sudden stops, capital flight, currency crises, and austerity — a pattern experienced by Mexico (1994), Asia (1997), Russia (1998), and Turkey (2018, 2021).

The 'capabilities approach' developed by Sen and Nussbaum proposes measuring development by 10 central human capabilities (health, bodily integrity, senses, emotions, practical reason, affiliation, other species, play, control over environment); the Multidimensional Poverty Index operationalizes a version of this, finding 1.1 billion people in multidimensional poverty.

The 'global labor arbitrage' — multinational corporations moving production to lower-wage countries — has driven extraordinary manufacturing cost reductions but also suppressed wages in origin countries; Apple's iPhone assembler Foxconn employed 1.4 million workers in China at peak, with average wages of $1–3/hour, illustrating the global wage-labor integration.

The 'Prebisch-Rosenstein-Rodan-Murphy' 'big push' model was tested by Muralidharan and Niehaus's (2017) study of a massive transfer program in Bihar, India, which showed that large-scale capital transfers to the ultra-poor (livestock, training, mentoring, food stipends) produced self-sustaining income gains 7 years later — empirical support for the big push mechanism.

The 'economic theory of marriage' (Becker, 1973) treats marriage as a matching market where individuals maximize utility through partner selection; it predicts increased divorce when women's economic independence rises (lower gains from specialization) and positive assortative mating (high earners marrying high earners) — both confirmed empirically as drivers of income inequality.

The 'global poverty data revolution' — high-frequency mobile-survey poverty measurement in developing countries — has transformed development economics; the World Bank's SWIFT (Survey of Wellbeing via Instant and Frequent Tracking) system can estimate poverty rates within 24 hours using mobile phone data, enabling real-time monitoring of social programs.

The 'secular increase in housing costs' in productive cities reflects both rising demand (agglomeration economies attracting workers) and restricted supply (zoning limiting new construction); economists Hsieh and Moretti (2019) estimated that deregulating zoning in just three U.S. cities (New York, San Francisco, San Jose) would raise U.S. GDP by 2% through better labor allocation.

The 'Prebisch-Patnaik' macroeconomics of capitalism with the state argued that capitalism's chronic tendency toward stagnation requires the state to maintain aggregate demand through military spending (arms Keynesianism), social programs, or public investment; this 'Keynesian dilemma' explains why full employment capitalism requires permanent government intervention.

The 'Great Divergence within countries' shows that regional inequality within nations often exceeds inequality between nations: in the U.S., per-capita GDP in San Jose is 5x that of Mississippi; in Italy, GDP per capita in Milan is 3x that of Palermo; in China, Shanghai's GDP per capita is 5x that of Gansu — creating political tensions that traditional macroeconomics overlooks.

The 'Prebisch-Gramsci' cultural hegemony approach to development argues that economic dependency is sustained not only through material power but through ideological dominance — the 'common sense' of markets, free trade, and Western development models is itself a form of intellectual dependency that constrains policy options in the Global South.

The 'future of work' research consistently finds that while automation eliminates some jobs, it also increases demand for human-complementary skills — creativity, empathy, complex problem-solving; the World Economic Forum predicts the 5 fastest-growing occupations to 2025 are AI/ML specialists, data analysts, digital marketing, renewable energy engineers, and care workers.

The 'participatory budgeting' movement — pioneered in Porto Alegre, Brazil in 1989 — allows citizens to directly vote on budget allocations, improving targeting of public investment toward low-income communities; by 2012 over 1,500 cities globally had adopted participatory budgeting, improving government accountability and service delivery in poor neighborhoods.

The 'Prebisch-Quesnay' physiocratic legacy in development economics — that only primary production (agriculture, mining) creates real value while manufacturing and services merely transform it — persisted in policies that discouraged manufacturing investment in Africa through the 1980s, contributing to the continent's failure to industrialize as Asia did.

The 'global carbon budget' framework quantifies the remaining carbon emissions that are consistent with 1.5°C or 2°C of warming; the IPCC estimates we can emit only another 500 GtCO₂ for a 50% chance of staying below 1.5°C — at current rates, this budget will be exhausted in approximately 12 years, giving climate economics and policy an absolute deadline.

The 'Prebisch-Boeke' dual economy analysis noted that colonial Indonesia had two distinct economic systems operating side by side: a Western capitalist sector and a traditional subsistence sector that responded differently to economic incentives; this 'dual society' diagnosis influenced development economics' focus on the interaction of formal and informal sectors.

The 'social multiplier' of education spending has been documented by economists Card and Krueger: each $1 spent on Black school quality in the U.S. South before desegregation generated $2 in increased lifetime earnings — a 200% return; similar multipliers are found for early childhood education (Perry Preschool study: 7–12% annual return over lifetime).

The 'Prebisch-Piore' labor market segmentation theory argues that capitalist labor markets are not unified but divided into primary (stable, good wages, internal labor markets) and secondary (unstable, poor wages, high turnover) sectors; workers are allocated between sectors by factors beyond individual productivity, including race, gender, and immigration status.

The 'carbon leakage problem' — where climate policy in one jurisdiction causes emissions to shift to less regulated regions — is estimated to offset 5–30% of domestic emissions reductions; it is the primary justification for carbon border adjustment mechanisms and weakens the case for unilateral climate action without international coordination.

The 'economic theory of bureaucracy' (Niskanen, 1971) argued that bureaucrats maximize their bureau's budget rather than social welfare, leading to systematically oversized public agencies; while this public choice critique influenced Reagan-era deregulation, empirical tests find mixed support — public sector performance varies enormously with institutional design.

The 'Prebisch-Krugman' new economic geography model showed that manufacturing activity concentrates in 'core' regions when trade costs fall below a threshold — because agglomeration economies outweigh land costs; this 'catastrophic agglomeration' creates persistent regional divergence and explains the concentration of industry in coastal China, the U.S. coastal metros, and EU core regions.

The 'just transition' concept in climate economics — ensuring that workers and communities dependent on fossil fuel industries share fairly in the costs and benefits of decarbonization — is endorsed by the ILO, IMF, and most major climate agreements; coal-mining regions in Germany, Appalachia, and South Africa require targeted investment and social protection to manage the transition.

The 'endogenous theory of policy' in political economy holds that economic policy is not exogenously chosen by benevolent planners but emerges from competition among interest groups; major economic policies — tax cuts, trade protection, minimum wage laws — can be predicted more accurately by the distribution of political power than by economic efficiency analysis.

The 'Prebisch-Thirlwall-Setterfield' cumulative causation model of growth argues that regional and national divergence is the norm rather than convergence: high-growth regions attract resources, investment, and talent from low-growth ones in self-reinforcing spirals — explaining why Scotland diverges from Southeast England and the U.S. Rust Belt diverges from California.

The global impact of the 2022 Ukraine war on food economics was severe: Ukraine and Russia combined supply 25–30% of global wheat, 15% of corn, and 75% of sunflower oil; the war caused commodity prices to spike 30–60%, contributing to food crises across 40 countries and threatening to reverse a decade of hunger reduction in the Global South.

The 'Prebisch-Robinson' uneven development within capitalism describes how capitalism simultaneously develops some regions and underdevelops others — not through neglect but through active resource extraction and market creation; 'combined and uneven development' (Trotsky's concept, developed by Robinson) is a framework for understanding postcolonial economic geography.

The 'Prebisch-Shapiro-Stiglitz' efficiency wage theory argues that firms pay wages above market-clearing levels to reduce worker shirking, turnover, and adverse selection; this explains involuntary unemployment (workers want jobs at the going wage but can't find them) and is an alternative to traditional supply-demand unemployment models.

The 'Prebisch-Furtado-CEPAL' proposal for Latin American 'structural transformation' was operationalized in the 1950s–1960s through state-owned enterprises in steel (USIMINAS, CSN), petrochemicals (Petrobras, PEMEX), and electricity; these SOEs succeeded in industrializing but created fiscal burdens and technological dependence that contributed to the 1980s debt crisis.

The 'heterodox money view' emphasizes that banks create purchasing power ex nihilo when they extend credit, meaning that investment precedes saving rather than the reverse in a monetary economy; this 'circuit of capital' perspective — where money is endogenous — challenges traditional loanable funds models and has implications for fiscal deficits and investment policy.

The 'gender composition of the workforce' affects national productivity: countries where women are highly educated but locked out of labor markets due to discrimination have vast untapped economic potential; IMF research found that eliminating the gender gap in labor force participation could increase per-capita income by 35% in South Asia and 58% in the Middle East.

The 'Prebisch-Steindl' maturation of capitalism thesis argued that advanced capitalist economies suffer from chronic excess capacity and slow growth because oligopolistic firms prefer maintaining high prices and margins over expanding output; this 'stagnation tendency' was prescient about post-2008 secular stagnation.

The 'economic gains from migration' are among the largest untapped sources of global welfare: estimates suggest that allowing just 3% more of the world's population to migrate to wealthier countries would generate economic gains larger than eliminating all remaining trade barriers combined — making immigration liberalization the world's highest-return economic policy.

The 'Prebisch-Sweezy' monopoly capitalism thesis (Baran and Sweezy, 1966) argued that advanced capitalism is characterized by giant corporations generating economic surplus that cannot be profitably invested, leading to advertising, waste, militarism, and imperialism as 'absorption mechanisms' — a structural explanation of post-WWII U.S. capitalist dynamics.

The 'household economics' revolution (Becker, 1964) treated families as small firms allocating time and money across market and home production; it generated insights on fertility (children as durable goods), household division of labor, and the trade-off between women's market work and household production — laying theoretical groundwork for gender economics.

The 'economic history of slavery' shows extraordinary profitability for slaveholders: the antebellum U.S. slave trade valued enslaved people at $3–4 billion (roughly $100 billion today), representing a larger capital asset than all Northern manufacturing and railroads combined; the cotton economy produced by enslaved labor generated 60% of U.S. export earnings.

The 'Prebisch-Boserup' innovation under population pressure theory argued (contrary to Malthus) that population growth stimulates technological innovation in agriculture — farmers intensify production methods, invent new tools, and reorganize labor when land becomes scarce; Ester Boserup's 1965 work influenced development thinking on the relationship between population and technology.

The 'financialization of everyday life' describes how ordinary people are increasingly required to manage investment risk through 401(k)s, stock options, student loans, and adjustable-rate mortgages — transferring financial risk from institutions to households; this 'democratization of risk' without democratization of financial literacy contributed to the 2008 crisis.

The 'Prebisch-Rowthorn' deindustrialization thesis showed that as countries develop, the share of manufacturing in GDP and employment falls not because manufacturing declines but because service productivity grows faster, raising service sector employment; 'premature deindustrialization' in Africa and Latin America — occurring at lower income levels than in Asia — is a development risk.

The 'labor market tightness' of the post-COVID U.S. economy — with job openings exceeding unemployed workers for the first time in recorded history — gave workers bargaining power they hadn't had since the 1960s; real wages rose at the bottom of the distribution, reversing decades of wage compression, and 'the Great Resignation' showed workers' willingness to exit bad jobs.

The 'Prebisch-Harrod' dynamic instability of capitalism ('knife-edge' growth) showed that the equilibrium growth rate is inherently unstable — if actual growth exceeds warranted rate, boom continues indefinitely; if it falls below, recession deepens; Harrod's 1939 dynamic theory anticipated modern secular stagnation and provided the macro framework Keynes lacked.

The 'economic integration paradox' shows that deeper economic integration produces economic gains but also economic vulnerability: EU integration dramatically boosted intra-EU trade and incomes but also enabled rapid contagion during the 2010 debt crisis; the tradeoff between integration gains and vulnerability is a central debate in international economics.

The 'global tax competition' has dramatically lowered corporate tax rates: the world average effective corporate tax rate fell from 49% in 1985 to 23% in 2022; the OECD's Pillar Two global minimum of 15% aims to halt this race to the bottom; economists estimate it could reclaim $150–220 billion annually in tax revenues currently avoided by profit-shifting.

The 'Prebisch-Keynes-Kalecki' principle of effective demand — that investment determines saving (not the reverse) and that capitalist economies are demand-constrained — provides the theoretical foundation for expansionary fiscal policy; the 'paradox of thrift' and 'fallacy of composition' in macroeconomics both flow from this demand-side perspective.

The 'fading American Dream' is documented empirically: the share of U.S. children earning more than their parents fell from 90% for children born in 1940 to 50% for children born in 1980; economists Chetty et al. attribute this collapse not to reduced growth but to increased inequality distributing growth's gains to those already at the top.

The 'Prebisch-Kaldor' growth model distinguished between manufacturing (subject to increasing returns and Verdoorn's Law — output growth increases productivity) and services (constant returns); Kaldor's three growth laws predict that manufacturing growth drives overall growth, explaining why premature deindustrialization is harmful for developing countries.

The 'economics of the Great Barrington Declaration' illustrated the difficulty of weighing lives in health-economic trade-offs: protecting the vulnerable while allowing herd immunity in the young was proposed as a low-cost COVID strategy; economists who modeled it found the trade-offs between lives saved, economic activity, and long-run immunity were extremely sensitive to uncertain epidemiological parameters.

The 'Prebisch-Dosi' evolutionary economics framework treats the economy as an evolving system of routines, firms, and technologies subject to selection pressure rather than equilibrium optimization; it provides a richer account of innovation, industrial dynamics, and national competitiveness than neoclassical theory.

The 'Universal Basic Income debate' in 2024 gained new urgency with AI advancement: proponents argue that AI productivity gains could fund UBI while compensating displaced workers; skeptics argue UBI would reduce work incentives, be inflationary at scale, and that targeted programs are more cost-effective — the debate remains one of the most politically live in economics.

The 'Prebisch-Pollin' green economy synthesis argues that massive investment in clean energy and public transit can simultaneously address climate change, create jobs, and reduce inequality — a 'Green New Deal' approach that treats environmental sustainability and economic justice as complementary rather than conflicting objectives.

source.name: Pollin, Robert - University of Massachusetts Amherst

text: The 'Prebisch-Lazonick' shareholder value revolution — the shift from 'retain and invest' to 'downsize and distribute' corporate strategies beginning in the 1980s — increased dividends and share buybacks at the expense of R&D and worker wages; Lazonick estimates that U.S. corporations returned $8.2 trillion to shareholders through buybacks from 2005–2014, reducing productive investment.

The 'economics of happiness policy' — applying wellbeing research to guide policy — has been adopted by New Zealand (Wellbeing Budget, 2019), Scotland, Wales, and Finland; these frameworks move beyond GDP to track mental health, environmental sustainability, loneliness, and housing security as policy targets, representing the most significant shift in government accounting since GDP was introduced in the 1940s.

The 'Prebisch-Palma-Sunkel' structural transformation agenda for Latin America emphasized moving from low-value primary exports to higher-value manufacturing and technology products; Chile's copper processing strategy, Brazil's aircraft industry (Embraer), and Mexico's automotive cluster represent partial successes in this structural upgrading despite broader regional failures.

Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky's Prospect Theory (1979) showed that people value losses roughly twice as much as equivalent gains — a phenomenon called loss aversion — fundamentally challenging the classical expected utility framework and earning Kahneman the 2002 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics.

Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein's nudge theory, popularized in their 2008 book, demonstrated that default options powerfully shape behavior: switching retirement savings enrollment from opt-in to opt-out increased participation rates from roughly 50% to over 90% in multiple U.S. corporate settings.

source.name: Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness

text: The anchoring effect in economics, documented by Tversky and Kahneman, shows that arbitrary numbers influence economic judgments: when asked to spin a wheel landing on 10 or 65 before estimating the percentage of African nations in the UN, participants' estimates were systematically pulled toward those arbitrary anchors.

Hyperbolic discounting — the tendency to prefer smaller, sooner rewards over larger, later ones much more steeply than exponential discounting predicts — helps explain why people undersave for retirement, procrastinate on healthy behaviors, and make choices they later regret; it underpins time-inconsistent preferences in behavioral economics.

The Ultimatum Game — an experimental economics staple — consistently shows that humans reject unequal splits of money even at a cost to themselves; offers below roughly 20–25% of the total are typically rejected worldwide, violating the standard rational-actor prediction that any positive offer should be accepted.

George Akerlof's 1970 'Market for Lemons' paper showed that information asymmetry — where sellers know more about product quality than buyers — can cause markets to collapse: in used car markets, buyers' inability to distinguish good cars from lemons drives down prices, crowding out good cars and potentially destroying the market.

Michael Spence's signaling theory (1973) explained why costly signals — like college degrees — can be economically rational even if education imparts no productive skills, because high-ability workers use education to credibly distinguish themselves from low-ability workers in markets with asymmetric information.

Joseph Stiglitz and Andrew Weiss demonstrated in 1981 that credit markets with asymmetric information lead to credit rationing — lenders may refuse loans at any interest rate rather than raise rates, because higher rates attract riskier borrowers (adverse selection) and encourage riskier projects (moral hazard).

Ronald Coase's theorem (1960) states that when property rights are well-defined and transaction costs are zero, parties will bargain to an efficient outcome regardless of the initial allocation of rights — a result that highlights transaction costs as the central obstacle to private solutions for externalities.

Elinor Ostrom, the first woman to win the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics (2009), empirically demonstrated that communities can sustainably manage common-pool resources — fisheries, forests, irrigation systems — through locally devised rules, without requiring privatization or government control, refuting the tragedy of the commons as inevitable.

The Heckscher-Ohlin trade model predicts that countries export goods that intensively use their relatively abundant factors of production; the Leontief Paradox (1953) challenged this by showing the U.S. — the world's most capital-abundant country — exported more labor-intensive goods than it imported.

source.name: Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society

text: Paul Krugman's New Trade Theory (1979–1980) showed that even without comparative advantage, countries trade in similar goods because of economies of scale and consumers' love of variety — explaining why Germany and France both produce and import cars, which classical trade theory predicted should specialize completely.

The gravity model of trade — borrowed from Newtonian physics — predicts bilateral trade flows are proportional to the product of two countries' GDP and inversely proportional to the distance between them; it is one of the most empirically robust relationships in international economics, explaining roughly 60–70% of variation in trade flows.

The Balassa-Samuelson effect explains why price levels are systematically higher in richer countries: productivity grows faster in tradable sectors (manufacturing) than non-tradables (services), pushing up wages and prices throughout the economy, making non-traded services expensive relative to poor countries.

The trilemma of international finance — also called the impossible trinity — holds that a country cannot simultaneously maintain a fixed exchange rate, free capital movement, and an independent monetary policy; it must sacrifice one, which explains why the Bretton Woods system eventually collapsed in 1971 under capital flow pressures.

source.name: Journal of International Money and Finance

text: The Mundell-Fleming model extended Keynesian IS-LM analysis to open economies, showing that fiscal policy is effective under fixed exchange rates but ineffective under floating rates (where crowding out operates through the exchange rate), while monetary policy has the opposite effectiveness profile.

Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) adjustments dramatically reshape global economic rankings: China's GDP measured at market exchange rates was about $18 trillion in 2023, but at PPP it exceeded $34 trillion — making China the world's largest economy by PPP since 2016 according to the IMF.

The Dutch Disease describes how a natural resource boom can harm a country's manufacturing sector: large export revenues from oil or gas appreciate the exchange rate, making manufactured exports uncompetitive; the Netherlands experienced this after discovering natural gas in 1959, giving the phenomenon its name.

The resource curse hypothesis — that countries with abundant natural resources tend to have slower economic growth and worse development outcomes — is supported by cross-country evidence: oil-rich states often have weaker institutions, more conflict, and greater inequality than resource-poor neighbors, though Norway is a prominent counter-example through its sovereign wealth fund model.

Norway's Government Pension Fund Global — the world's largest sovereign wealth fund at over $1.7 trillion — was established in 1990 to invest oil revenues abroad, insulating the domestic economy from Dutch Disease and ensuring intergenerational equity; by 2023 it owned roughly 1.5% of all listed stocks globally.

Import Substitution Industrialization (ISI) — the development strategy of replacing imported manufactured goods with domestic production through tariffs and subsidies — was dominant in Latin America and Africa from the 1950s to 1970s; while it built industrial capacity, it often created inefficient industries dependent on continued protection and contributed to debt crises.

Export-Led Growth, the development model adopted by East Asian tiger economies — South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, and Hong Kong — deliberately oriented industries toward global markets rather than protecting them from competition, achieving sustained 8–10% annual growth for decades and rapid convergence toward developed-country income levels.

The Flying Geese model of economic development, proposed by Japanese economist Kaname Akamatsu in the 1930s and extended by scholars studying East Asia, describes how industries migrate from more advanced to less advanced countries as wages rise — Japan leading, followed by Korea and Taiwan, then ASEAN nations, and eventually China.

South Korea's industrial policy — channeling credit through state-owned banks to chaebols (large conglomerates) in targeted export sectors like steel, shipbuilding, and electronics — transformed the country from one of the world's poorest in 1960 ($80 GDP per capita) to a high-income OECD member by the 1990s in what economists call the Korean miracle.

The Washington Consensus — a set of ten market-liberalization policies advocated by Washington-based institutions (IMF, World Bank, U.S. Treasury) for developing countries in the 1980s and 1990s — included privatization, deregulation, trade liberalization, and fiscal discipline; critics argue its rigid application deepened recessions in countries like Argentina and contributed to lost decades of growth in Africa.

Financial dollarization — widespread use of a foreign currency (typically the U.S. dollar) as a store of value or medium of exchange alongside or instead of the domestic currency — leaves countries vulnerable to liability dollarization: when domestic currency depreciates, dollar-denominated debts become unpayable, as Ecuador found before formally adopting the dollar in 2000.

The 1994 Mexican Tequila Crisis — triggered when Mexico devalued the peso after years of running current account deficits financed by short-term capital inflows — spread rapidly to Argentina and other emerging markets, demonstrating the contagion effect where financial crises jump between countries through investor panic and capital flight.

The 1997–1998 Asian Financial Crisis began when Thailand floated the baht in July 1997 after defending an overvalued peg exhausted foreign reserves; the crisis spread to Indonesia, South Korea, and Malaysia, causing GDP contractions of 5–15%, and prompted an IMF bailout package exceeding $100 billion, with controversial austerity conditions that deepened recessions.

Argentina's 2001 default — at $100 billion the largest sovereign debt default in history at that time — came after a decade of currency board peg to the dollar caused deflation and recession; the corralito banking freeze preventing withdrawals triggered riots, five presidents in two weeks, and a 10–11% economic collapse in 2002.

Modern Monetary Theory (MMT), associated with economists Stephanie Kelton and Warren Mosler, argues that currency-issuing governments face no financial constraint on spending in their own currency — they can always create money — and that the real constraints are inflation and resource availability; mainstream economists largely reject MMT's policy prescriptions as inflationary.

The Quantity Theory of Money — summarized in MV = PQ (money supply times velocity equals price level times output) — underpins monetarism and provided the theoretical basis for the inflation-fighting policies of central banks in the 1980s, though the velocity of money has proven unstable in practice, undermining simple monetarist predictions.

The Taylor Rule, proposed by economist John Taylor in 1993, prescribes how central banks should set interest rates based on deviations of inflation from target and output from potential; despite being a simple formula, it describes Federal Reserve behavior remarkably well in the 1980s–2000s and is widely used as a benchmark for monetary policy assessment.

source.name: Carnegie-Rochester Conference Series on Public Policy

text: Zero-lower-bound monetary policy — the situation where nominal interest rates cannot be cut below zero — became a central challenge after the 2008 crisis, prompting central banks to adopt unconventional tools: quantitative easing (asset purchases), forward guidance, and negative interest rates.

Quantitative Easing (QE) — large-scale central bank asset purchases to inject liquidity when interest rates are at zero — was first deployed by the Bank of Japan after 2001, then broadly by the Federal Reserve ($4.5 trillion in assets by 2015), ECB, and Bank of England after 2008; research suggests QE lowered long-term yields by 0.5–1.5 percentage points.

Inflation targeting — adopted first by New Zealand in 1990 and subsequently by the U.K., Canada, and eventually most major central banks — commits monetary policy to maintaining inflation near a publicly announced target (typically 2%), enhancing transparency and anchoring expectations; it is credited with the Great Moderation of reduced inflation volatility from the mid-1980s to 2007.

The Lucas Critique (1976) — Robert Lucas's argument that econometric models based on historical relationships break down when policy changes, because agents change their behavior in response to policy — fundamentally reshaped macroeconomics, contributing to the shift toward microfounded models (DSGE models) with explicit optimization by rational agents.

text: Real Business Cycle (RBC) theory, developed by Finn Kydland and Edward Prescott (Nobel 2004), explained economic fluctuations as optimal responses to real shocks (technology changes) rather than monetary or demand disturbances; while analytically influential, RBC models were criticized for implying that recessions are efficient and unemployment is voluntary.

New Keynesian economics — the synthesis of Keynesian demand-side insights with microeconomic foundations — incorporates price stickiness, imperfect competition, and monetary non-neutrality into rational-expectations models; DSGE (Dynamic Stochastic General Equilibrium) models built on this framework became the standard tool at major central banks by the 2000s.

Secular stagnation — the hypothesis revived by Larry Summers in 2013 drawing on Alvin Hansen's 1938 concept — argues that advanced economies may face persistently weak demand, low interest rates, and slow growth due to demographic aging, declining investment needs, and rising savings; the 2010s decade of near-zero interest rates in Europe and Japan lent it credibility.

The Solow Residual — the portion of economic growth unexplained by increases in labor or capital inputs — was estimated by Robert Solow (1957) to account for roughly 80% of U.S. output growth per worker from 1909 to 1949, suggesting technological progress (total factor productivity) is the dominant driver of long-run living standards.

Paul Romer's Endogenous Growth Theory (1986, 1990) made technological change a result of purposeful investment in research and development rather than an unexplained external force; because knowledge is non-rival and partly non-excludable, it generates positive spillovers and explains how economies can sustain growth without diminishing returns to capital.

Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson, and James Robinson's settler mortality instrument (2001) used historical data on European colonist death rates to show that colonies with healthier environments developed more inclusive institutions — which persistently raised income — providing some of the strongest evidence that institutions, not geography or culture, cause economic development.

Convergence theory in economics — the prediction that poorer countries grow faster than rich ones because capital has higher marginal returns where it is scarce — finds support in conditional convergence: controlling for savings rates, population growth, and institutions, countries do converge; unconditional convergence across all countries is weaker.

The Big Push theory of development, associated with Paul Rosenstein-Rodan (1943) and later Murphy, Shleifer, and Vishny (1989), argues that low-income countries can be trapped in underdevelopment when no individual firm finds it profitable to industrialize, but coordinated simultaneous investment by many firms creates the market demand to make each individual investment profitable.

The Prebisch-Singer hypothesis (1950), independently proposed by Raul Prebisch and Hans Singer, argued that the terms of trade for primary commodity exporters deteriorate over time relative to manufactured goods exporters — a controversial claim that underpinned calls for industrialization and provided intellectual foundations for UNCTAD.

The gender wage gap — the difference in median earnings between men and women — persists across all economies; in OECD countries it averaged about 12% in 2022 when measured as full-time employee earnings, though much of the gap reflects occupational segregation, industry differences, and working hours rather than direct pay discrimination for identical work.

Claudia Goldin's research on the last chapter of the gender earnings gap — awarded the 2023 Nobel in Economics — showed that a large share of the remaining gap reflects greedy jobs: occupations (finance, corporate law, medicine) that pay disproportionately for long, inflexible hours, penalizing caregivers who are disproportionately women.

The automation and labor displacement debate intensified with research by Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo showing that each additional robot in U.S. manufacturing from 1990–2007 reduced employment by 3–6 workers and lowered wages in affected commuting zones, challenging the view that automation always creates as many jobs as it destroys.

Polarization of the labor market — documented by economists David Autor, Frank Levy, and Richard Murnane — shows that employment and wages have grown most in high-skill cognitive jobs and low-skill manual service jobs, while middle-skill routine jobs in manufacturing and clerical work have declined, creating an hourglass labor market.

The Beveridge Curve — the empirical relationship between the job vacancy rate and the unemployment rate — typically shows a negative correlation as labor markets tighten; shifts in the curve (more unemployment for a given vacancy rate) indicate matching inefficiency, and the 2021–2022 rightward shift after COVID-19 signaled structural mismatch in U.S. labor markets.

text: The Phillips Curve — the inverse relationship between unemployment and inflation postulated by A.W. Phillips in 1958 — was central to economic policymaking until Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps independently showed in 1968 that the relationship only holds in the short run; in the long run, there is no exploitable trade-off as inflation expectations adjust.

The NAIRU (Non-Accelerating Inflation Rate of Unemployment) — the unemployment rate at which inflation is stable — is estimated to be around 4–5% in the United States, though it varies over time; attempts to push unemployment below the NAIRU through expansionary policy tend to generate accelerating inflation rather than sustained low unemployment.

Hysteresis in labor markets — the idea that temporarily high unemployment becomes permanent through skill atrophy, long-term unemployment stigma, and reduced job search — was proposed to explain European unemployment persistence in the 1980s; it implies that recessions can permanently raise the natural rate of unemployment if not combated aggressively.

Monopsony power in labor markets — where employers have wage-setting power over workers — received renewed empirical attention after economists showed that labor markets are highly concentrated in many sectors; research suggests monopsony power may suppress wages by 10–20% below competitive levels and provides new justifications for minimum wages.

Efficiency wages — the theory that firms may voluntarily pay above market-clearing wages to increase worker productivity through reduced turnover, better worker effort, and adverse selection avoidance — helps explain why wages do not fall to eliminate unemployment during recessions, contributing to the Keynesian understanding of wage rigidity.

The Lewis Model of development (1954) described how labor-surplus economies grow by transferring disguised unemployment from subsistence agriculture to a modern industrial sector; the model explains the early stage of East Asian growth but predicts a Lewis turning point when surplus labor is exhausted and wages begin to rise.

China's Lewis turning point — the exhaustion of surplus rural labor — occurred roughly around 2010–2012, as evidenced by rising rural wages and reduced migration to urban factories; it marked a structural shift in China's development model from cheap-labor export manufacturing toward higher-value-added production and consumption-driven growth.

Health capital theory, developed by Michael Grossman (1972), treats health as a durable capital stock that depreciates over time and can be augmented by investing in medical care, diet, and exercise — providing a microeconomic framework for analyzing health behaviors and explaining why demand for health care rises with education and wages.

The Oregon Health Insurance Experiment (2008–2010) — a rare randomized controlled trial of Medicaid expansion using a lottery — found that Medicaid coverage significantly improved financial security and mental health but showed no statistically significant effect on clinical outcomes like blood pressure or diabetes control after two years.

The RAND Health Insurance Experiment (1974–1982) — one of the most expensive social science experiments ever conducted — found that people with free health care used significantly more medical services than those with cost-sharing, but among the non-poor showed similar health outcomes, providing foundational evidence on health insurance demand elasticity.

source.name: Health Insurance and the Demand for Medical Care

text: U.S. health expenditure exceeded 17% of GDP in 2022 — roughly double the OECD average — yet health outcomes including life expectancy, infant mortality, and disease management rank near the bottom of wealthy nations, reflecting what economists call the American health care cost paradox.

The value of a statistical life (VSL) — the monetary value implicit in safety regulations and risk reductions — is estimated by the U.S. EPA at roughly $11–12 million (2023 dollars), derived from wage premiums workers demand for risky jobs; it is used to evaluate regulations on pollution, road safety, and product standards.

source.name: EPA Guidelines for Preparing Economic Analyses

text: Pigouvian taxes — named after economist Arthur Pigou who formalized the theory in 1920 — correct market failures by taxing activities that generate negative externalities (pollution, carbon) at a rate equal to the marginal social damage, making private costs equal social costs; they are considered economically efficient instruments for environmental policy.

The Social Cost of Carbon (SCC) — the monetary value of damages from emitting one additional ton of CO2 — was estimated by the U.S. government at about $51 per ton under the Obama administration, reduced to $1 under Trump, and raised to $190 per ton by Biden in 2023 following National Academies recommendations; the figure shapes climate policy cost-benefit calculations.

The EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) — launched in 2005 as the world's first large-scale carbon market — covers about 40% of EU greenhouse gas emissions from power plants and heavy industry; after initial price collapses caused by over-allocation of permits, reforms introduced a Market Stability Reserve in 2019, pushing prices above 80 euros per tonne by 2022.

British Columbia's carbon tax, introduced in 2008 at $10 per tonne and rising to $65 per tonne by 2022, is widely studied as an early example of a carbon price combined with revenue recycling (tax cuts elsewhere); research found it reduced BC's gasoline consumption by 15% and per-capita emissions by 5–15% relative to trends, without measurable harm to economic growth.

source.name: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

text: Green national accounting — extending GDP to include environmental degradation and natural capital depletion — has been advanced by the System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) adopted by the UN in 2012; estimates suggest green GDP in resource-intensive economies like China is 2–5% lower than conventional GDP when pollution and resource depletion are included.

Ecosystem services valuation — assigning economic values to benefits nature provides such as pollination, water purification, and carbon storage — was popularized by Robert Costanza et al.'s 1997 paper estimating total global ecosystem services at $33 trillion annually (larger than global GDP at the time), galvanizing the field of ecological economics.

The Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) hypothesis predicts that pollution first rises as countries develop, then falls after income reaches a threshold — typically $5,000–$8,000 GDP per capita — as citizens demand cleaner environments and economies shift to services; evidence supports the EKC for local pollutants like sulfur dioxide but not for CO2 and other global pollutants.

source.name: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management

text: Stranded assets in fossil fuels — the stock of coal, oil, and gas reserves that would become economically or legally unburnable under climate policies consistent with 2 degrees Celsius warming — are estimated at $1–4 trillion globally; the carbon bubble concept warns that financial markets may be overvaluing fossil fuel companies that cannot monetize these reserves.

Climate change is projected to reduce global GDP by 10–23% by 2100 under high-emissions scenarios according to estimates by Burke, Hsiang, and Miguel (2015) using historical temperature-GDP relationships, though estimates vary widely; tropical and poorer regions face the largest losses, raising major distributional and justice questions in climate economics.

The 2008 global financial crisis originated in the U.S. subprime mortgage market: financial innovation (mortgage-backed securities, collateralized debt obligations) had spread toxic mortgage risk throughout the global financial system while credit rating agencies systematically mispriced it; the collapse of Lehman Brothers on September 15, 2008, triggered a global credit freeze.

Too-Big-to-Fail (TBTF) — the implicit government guarantee that systemically important financial institutions will be rescued — creates moral hazard: these banks take excessive risks knowing losses will be socialized; post-2008 reforms including Dodd-Frank's living wills and higher capital requirements for G-SIBs (global systemically important banks) attempted to address TBTF.

Shadow banking — financial intermediation by non-bank entities including money market funds, hedge funds, repo markets, and securitization vehicles — grew to exceed $70 trillion globally before the 2008 crisis, performing bank-like maturity transformation without deposit insurance or central bank backstops, making it vulnerable to bank-run dynamics.

The Minsky Moment — named after economist Hyman Minsky who argued that stability breeds instability — describes the sudden collapse of asset prices when speculators who borrowed to buy assets are forced to sell; Minsky classified borrowers as hedge (income covers debt), speculative (needs refinancing), or Ponzi (relies on asset appreciation), predicting crisis when Ponzi finance dominates.

Basel III — the international banking regulatory framework developed in response to the 2008 crisis by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision — required banks to hold higher quality capital (Common Equity Tier 1 of at least 4.5% of risk-weighted assets), introduced a leverage ratio, and created liquidity requirements to reduce bank fragility.

Reinhart and Rogoff's 'This Time Is Different' (2009) analyzed 800 years of financial crises, finding that sovereign debt crises, banking crises, and currency crises follow remarkably similar patterns across time and countries, typically causing GDP to fall 9% below trend and unemployment to remain elevated for 7 years or more after the crisis.

The Great Moderation (1984–2007) — a period of reduced macroeconomic volatility in the U.S. and other developed economies with low, stable inflation and mild recessions — was attributed by Ben Bernanke to better monetary policy, structural changes, and good luck; the 2008 crisis abruptly ended it, raising questions about whether it reflected suppressed rather than reduced risk.

The Eurozone sovereign debt crisis (2010–2015) revealed structural flaws in the euro: member countries shared monetary policy but retained fiscal policy, and when Greek, Irish, and Portuguese governments faced markets doubting their solvency, they lacked lender-of-last-resort support until ECB President Draghi's whatever it takes pledge in July 2012 calmed bond markets.

Optimum Currency Area theory, developed by Robert Mundell (1961), identifies conditions under which sharing a currency is beneficial: high factor mobility, trade openness, economic symmetry, and fiscal transfer mechanisms; by these criteria the Eurozone was considered sub-optimal — lacking a common fiscal policy and with limited labor mobility — which became evident during the sovereign debt crisis.

Austerity economics — the theory that fiscal consolidation (spending cuts and tax increases) can be expansionary by reducing interest rates and improving private sector confidence — was advocated widely after 2010; subsequent research, including IMF studies by Olivier Blanchard, found fiscal multipliers were larger than assumed (1.5 rather than 0.5), meaning austerity substantially deepened European recessions.

The loanable funds theory holds that interest rates equilibrate savings supply and investment demand in a competitive market; Keynes challenged this with the liquidity preference theory, arguing interest rates are determined by money supply and demand for liquidity — a debate that remains alive in macroeconomics between classical and Keynesian paradigms.

text: The IS-LM model — developed by John Hicks (1937) to formalize Keynes's General Theory — describes short-run macroeconomic equilibrium where the goods market (IS curve) and money market (LM curve) simultaneously clear; despite criticism for over-simplifying, it remains a widely taught pedagogical framework for analyzing fiscal and monetary policy interactions.

The Keynesian multiplier — the idea that an initial increase in government spending raises income by a multiple of the original spending as money circulates through the economy — depends on the marginal propensity to consume (MPC); if MPC is 0.8, the multiplier is 5 (1 divided by (1 minus 0.8)), though real-world multipliers are smaller due to leakages, crowding out, and openness.

text: Ricardian Equivalence — proposed by David Ricardo and formalized by Robert Barro (1974) — argues that rational taxpayers, anticipating that government debt today means higher taxes tomorrow, reduce current consumption to save for future tax payments, neutralizing the stimulative effect of deficit-financed tax cuts; empirical support for this strong result is limited.

The Permanent Income Hypothesis, developed by Milton Friedman (1957), states that consumers base spending decisions on their estimated permanent (long-run average) income rather than current income, implying temporary income changes have smaller consumption effects than permanent changes; this helps explain why one-time tax rebates have modest stimulative effects.

source.name: A Theory of the Consumption Function

text: Thorstein Veblen's concept of conspicuous consumption (1899) described how wealthy consumers buy expensive goods not for utility but to signal status — Veblen goods are those where demand increases as price rises, the inverse of normal goods; Veblen's critique of leisure-class economics anticipated sociological and behavioral economics by decades.

source.name: The Theory of the Leisure Class

text: John Kenneth Galbraith's 'The Affluent Society' (1958) argued that post-war America's private opulence coexisted with public squalor: high consumer spending on luxury goods alongside underfunded schools, infrastructure, and public services; his concept of the dependence effect — advertising creating the wants it then satisfies — challenged the assumption of sovereign consumer preferences.

Friedrich von Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945) argued that prices in market economies aggregate dispersed, local, tacit knowledge that no central planner could possess — providing the theoretical foundation for market economies' informational superiority over central planning and shaping the critique of Soviet-style command economies.

The Socialist Calculation Debate of the 1930s pitted Ludwig von Mises and Hayek (who argued rational calculation was impossible without market prices) against Oskar Lange (who proposed a market socialist model using trial-and-error price-setting); the debate remained largely theoretical until the collapse of Soviet planning appeared to vindicate the Mises-Hayek position.

Amartya Sen's Capability Approach — developed through works including 'Poverty and Famines' (1981) and 'Development as Freedom' (1999) — reframes economic development as expansion of substantive freedoms and human capabilities rather than income growth alone; it underpins the UN Human Development Index (HDI) which combines income, education, and life expectancy.

The Human Development Index (HDI), published annually in UNDP's Human Development Report since 1990 and designed by Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen, ranks countries by a composite of income, education, and life expectancy; Norway has topped the index most years, while the index has helped shift development discourse away from GDP-only metrics.

The Kuznets Curve — Simon Kuznets's 1955 hypothesis that income inequality first rises and then falls as countries develop (an inverted U) — provided an optimistic view that growth automatically reduces inequality; empirical evidence is mixed, with many countries moving along the curve's rising portion without reaching the turning point.

Doughnut Economics, proposed by Kate Raworth (2017), visualizes a safe and just space for humanity between a social foundation (meeting all human needs) and an ecological ceiling (staying within planetary boundaries); it explicitly rejects GDP growth as the primary goal and proposes regenerative, distributive economies as the design objective.

Degrowth economics — advocating deliberate reduction of economic output in wealthy nations to reduce environmental impact and improve well-being — challenges the growth imperative in mainstream economics; proponents argue GDP growth in rich countries no longer improves well-being and comes at unsustainable ecological cost, while critics argue growth is needed to finance the green transition.

The Easterlin Paradox — named after economist Richard Easterlin who observed in 1974 that within countries richer people are happier, but over time countries do not become happier as they grow richer — challenged the assumption that income growth improves well-being; it spurred the happiness economics field, though later research using larger datasets has questioned the paradox.

source.name: Nations and Households in Economic Growth

text: The economics of information goods — software, music, books — differs fundamentally from physical goods because they have near-zero marginal reproduction costs but high fixed production costs; this creates natural monopoly tendencies, makes traditional price-equals-marginal-cost efficiency impossible, and drives platform economics built on network effects.

Platform economics and two-sided markets — analyzed by Jean Tirole and Jean-Charles Rochet — involve platforms serving distinct groups (buyers and sellers, readers and advertisers) that create value for each other; platform pricing is often subsidized on one side (readers get free content) and monetized on the other (advertisers pay), making traditional competition analysis inadequate.

The economics of superstar markets — proposed by Sherwin Rosen in 1981 — explains extreme earnings concentration at the top of talent distributions: small differences in ability translate into large earnings differences when technology allows the best performers to serve mass markets at low marginal cost, explaining why top singers, athletes, and executives earn thousands of times more than average performers.

Adam Smith's invisible hand — perhaps the most famous metaphor in economics, appearing just three times across his works — describes how individuals pursuing private interests unintentionally promote social welfare through market competition; Smith himself was careful to note its limitations and devoted much of 'The Wealth of Nations' to cases where markets fail to serve the public interest, including monopoly, collusion, and the neglect of public goods.
